title: ZenFold pilot: weekly economics & tuning sync

quantization effects on latency and quality
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on pilot economics: Redwood presented batch and caching sensitivity runs. Key takeaways: KV/prefix caching yields ~18-30% cost improvement depending on prompt locality; batching improves throughput but adds tail latency (tradeoff varies by batch size); quantization saved compute cost with modest quality delta. Next steps agreed: share updated pilot-results.csv, customer provides production trace, and schedule a Dedicated capacity stress test.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-05 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Santos (ZenFold CTO), Laura Kim (ZenFold ML), Jared Ortiz (ZenFold Infra)

Summary (auto): Weekly pilot check-in; cost/unit economics deep-dive; decisions on batching/caching experiments.

00:00:03 Alex Chen: all right everyone uh welcome back to the weekly pilot sync for ZenFold, Alex from Redwood here, with Priya from our SE team. How are we doing Mark?
00:00:11 Mark Santos: Good, good thanks. We pulled in Laura and Jared for the cost stuff. We've skimmed the deck you sent, but want to go deeper on the tokens per dollar things.
00:00:21 Priya Nair: Yep, today we'll walk through the sensitivity runs we ran this week — batching, K V cache sizing, and a quick quantization pass — and then align on the Dedicated stress test. Note: some numbers are approximate from the telemetry.

00:01:05 Alex Chen: Quick recap — baseline hosted run with batch size 1 and no prefix cache gave about 480 tokens/sec/$ for the chosen model variant. When we enabled prefix/K-V caching tuned to the prompt locality, we saw tokens/sec/$ move to ~620, so roughly a 29% uplift. Caveat: your workload has a 38% prefix overlap which made caching more effective.
00:01:42 Laura Kim: Wait 480 tokens per second per dollar? Just to check units — that's tokens/sec per dollar spent as averaged over the hour, right?
00:01:50 Priya Nair: Yup, it's tokens/sec/$ averaged. The way we compute: tokens served divided by compute cost in dollars over the sampling window, normalized by the median observed p99 latency window. It's a composite metric so it's easier to compare configs.

00:02:26 Mark Santos: Those uplift numbers look promising. Can you walk us through the batching tradeoffs — we have strict 200–400ms RTT needs for the interactive flow.
00:02:36 Priya Nair: Absolutely. With batch size 1 median latency was ~110ms, p95 ~220ms. When we moved to batched inference with batch=8, throughput improved ~2.4x (so tokens/sec/$ up around 2.3x), but median latency shifted to ~320ms and p95 to ~630ms. So big cost win but we cross your 400ms threshold on median.

00:03:20 Jared Ortiz: Did you test hybrid batching where small requests are served as low-latency and large bursts batch?
00:03:25 Priya Nair: We did a small experiment — dynamic batching by priority. For the interactive route we kept max batch size of 2 with aggressive timeout (6ms) and got a 20% throughput boost while staying under 180ms median. For background bulk jobs we allowed batch=8 and got the high throughput. That's the recommended config for mixed workloads.

00:04:10 Alex Chen: Another nuance — KV/prefix cache savings are very sensitive to sequence length and prefix repetition. For your 38% prefix re-use and avg seq 240 tokens we estimated end-to-end token cost savings ~18% on average, up to 30% in high locality endpoints.
00:04:33 Laura Kim: Any tooling to validate prefix locality in production? We need to convince our product folks before we ship.
00:04:40 Priya Nair: Yes — we include a small diagnostics script in the pilot repo that scans request traces and emits prefix reuse heatmaps. We'll attach that to the pilot-results.csv. It's the same one we used to estimate the 38%.

00:05:15 Mark Santos: On quantization — you mentioned an 8-bit run gave some latency/cost benefits. How big was the quality delta?
00:05:23 Priya Nair: The 8-bit quant runs reduced per-token compute cost by ~15% in our internal bench and trimmed latency by ~10–12%. In the eval set we saw a small drop in Rouge/bleu-like proxy (we use a semantic-similarity eval) — roughly a 1.5–2% relative drop on edge cases. For many of your templates it's within tolerance, but Laura will want to validate on your prompts.
00:06:05 Laura Kim: We'll need a quick A/B on our prompt set; can we get the quantized variant exposed in the pilot?
00:06:11 Alex Chen: Yes we can expose it as model: model-xyz-quant8 in the pilot catalog. We'll mark it as quality-flagged so it won't be auto-rolled to prod.

00:06:48 Jared Ortiz: Regarding Dedicated testing — we want to validate the economics at 10k qps sustained. Can Redwood replicate tokens/sec/$ at that scale?
00:06:56 Priya Nair: We can. The Dedicated pool has predictable throughput; our expectation is tokens/sec/$ is slightly better on Dedicated due to fixed occupancy and better batching efficiency. In the small Dedicated run we did last month, tokens/sec/$ improved ~12% vs hosted for the same configs (batching allowed higher effective utilization). We'll need the VPC peering confirmed to run the end-to-end test.

00:07:35 Mark Santos: Cost model question — does your model include network egress and tokenization overheads? We saw a gap in the first spreadsheet where network costs were omitted.
00:07:44 Alex Chen: Good catch. The sheet in the first pass omitted cross-region egress, which is relevant for your distributed frontends. We'll update the model to include egress and a separate line for tokenization CPU overhead. Expect that in the updated CSV.

00:08:18 Laura Kim: On telemetry — what's the retention period for per-token logs during the pilot? We need them for our billing reconciliation and quality checks but cannot retain PII.
00:08:28 Alex Chen: Pilot defaults to 30 days retention in the Console; we can increase retention for troubleshooting. All logs can be anonymized and Redwood supports KMS encryption. We'll send the security summary doc (SOC2 sections) as an addendum.

00:09:02 Mark Santos: ok good. Another thought: the cost delta on caching — is that realized on tokens or on GPU cycles? Meaning, do you avoid decoding tokens or do you avoid compute across attention?
00:09:14 Priya Nair: Practically it's avoided compute — the KV cache reduces repeated attention work; you still pay for the final decode tokens, but per-request compute is much lower. So it's a mix: fewer GPU cycles per input and fewer memory ops which shows up in the billing as lower compute consumption.

00:10:00 Alex Chen: A note on tail latency — caching can slightly increase variance because cache hits are fast but misses fall back to full decode path. We saw a bimodal latency distribution in the traces we shared; we'll annotate pilot-results.csv with the hit/miss latencies per route.

00:11:12 Mark Santos: Can we try a conservative config for our interactive route: keep batch<=2, aggressive timeout, quantization disabled initially, prefix cache enabled with conservative TTL?
00:11:22 Priya Nair: Yes that's in line with what we recommended. That config in our test had median ~140ms and tokens/sec/$ about 1.25x baseline.

00:12:05 Laura Kim: For the bulk batch job (inference for nightly jobs) we can accept higher latency. Can you produce expected savings chart for batch=8 vs batch=16?
00:12:14 Priya Nair: We have that in the sensitivity runs. Quick preview: batch=8 gave ~2.3x tokens/sec/$ vs batch=1; batch=16 gave ~2.6x but diminishing returns on marginal improvement and bigger tails on p99. We'll put the chart in the CSV as separate columns.

00:13:01 Jared Ortiz: Are there any production gotchas for memory overhead with batch=16? We run with limited GPU memory headroom.
00:13:09 Priya Nair: Yes batch size increases KV and activation memory; on larger batches peak GPU memory can go up 25–40% depending on sequence length. If your GPUs are memory-tight, we recommend batch=8 or using a quantized variant to reduce memory footprint.

00:14:00 Alex Chen: Quick bit on routing: Redwood's routing can pin interactive traffic to lower-batch, low-latency hosts and route background to high-batch hosts; that gives you a consistent SLAT profile while optimizing total tokens/$ across the fleet. You can set policy by route, model, or label.

00:14:36 Mark Santos: Sounds good. For the Dedicated run we'll need to sign off on SLA windows and test certificates. Jared will coordinate.

00:15:10 Jared Ortiz: I'll try to open a 2-hour window next Tuesday night PST for the test. I need Redwood accounts setup for the peering. Also, we'll need the firewall IPs.
00:15:20 Alex Chen: We'll provide a one-pager with required IPs, ports and a short playbook for peering; dropping it into the shared folder after this call.

00:16:02 Laura Kim: Can we get a short explanation of how tokens/sec/$ changes with model size? Our experimental model is medium-size but we might consider a smaller distilled variant.
00:16:12 Priya Nair: In general smaller models have a higher tokens/sec/$ but may require more evals for quality tradeoffs. In our chart: large model baseline tokens/sec/$ was 420; medium variant was 480; small distilled variant reached ~730 tokens/sec/$ but with higher error rate on some prompts. We'll share the size-vs-economics chart.

00:17:05 Mark Santos: One more ask — can we get the raw traces from the earlier Dedicated run you mentioned? We want to look at p99 and batching behavior.
00:17:13 Priya Nair: Yes we'll attach anonymized traces to the pilot-results.zip. They include per-request latencies and whether it was a cache hit or miss.

00:18:00 Alex Chen: Quick pause — transcription note: some system auto captions may show "dedecated" or K V cache as K-V space; ignore that in the csv.
00:18:08 Mark Santos: haha noted.

00:18:25 Laura Kim: On the action timeline — after we get the updated CSV and the 1k request trace, we'll schedule a 2-week run with mixed traffic. Does Redwood support automated rollout to production if we like the results?
00:18:36 Alex Chen: Yes we support canary and percent-based rollouts in Console. For pilots we'll keep it manual; if you choose to proceed to prod we can automate a staged rollout with rollback thresholds on latency and quality regressions.

00:19:12 Jared Ortiz: Regarding security, we need to review the SOC2 details you mentioned and the KMS integration. Can you share your SOC2 summary and the KMS integration doc?
00:19:21 Alex Chen: Yes — I'll attach SOC2-excerpt.pdf and KMS-integration.md to the follow-up.

00:20:00 Mark Santos: Anything else on economics? I want to be sure we didn't miss hidden costs: tokenization CPU, network egress, idle dedicated costs.
00:20:10 Priya Nair: We'll add tokenization as a line item and an optional egress estimator. For Dedicated we present both amortized per-hour and fully-loaded per-token numbers so you can decide on cost model.

00:21:02 Alex Chen: Alright, let's recap next steps. We'll: (1) update pilot-results.csv with more columns for batch sizes (1,2,8,16), cache hit/miss latencies, tokens/sec/$, and dedicated run traces; (2) attach the diagnostics script for prefix locality and the quantized variant model endpoint; (3) schedule Dedicated stress test with Jared.

00:21:32 Mark Santos: Sounds good. Laura and I will provide the 1k trace and prompt set by Monday.
00:21:40 Laura Kim: Yes, aiming to get it to you by end of day Monday.

00:22:05 Jared Ortiz: I'll confirm peering window and firewall rules by Friday.

00:22:30 Alex Chen: Great. Any blockers?
00:22:35 Mark Santos: Not from our side; just want to validate numbers in the CSV.
00:22:40 Priya Nair: We'll annotate assumptions in the CSV (e.g., seq length, reuse %, model variant, region pricing).

00:23:00 Alex Chen: Ok we'll follow up with the artifacts after the call. Thanks everyone.
00:23:06 Mark Santos: Thanks.
00:23:10 Laura Kim: Thanks all.

[End of transcript — remaining ~19 minutes used for side-channel infra config chat and screen-sharing the CSV; those details saved in pilot-results.csv and infra-playbook.pdf in shared drive]
